Here \(f(3) = 3^2 + 2 = 11\), and \(\lim\limits_{x\to 3^-}(6x-7) = 11\), so f is continuous at \(x=3\). Continuity alone is not enough, so compare the two one-sided derivatives.
Left-hand derivative (using \(f(x)=6x-7\) for \(x<3\)):
\(Lf'(3) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^-}\frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^-}\frac{[6(3+h)-7]-11}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^-}\frac{6h}{h} = 6\).
Right-hand derivative (using \(f(x)=x^2+2\) for \(x\ge 3\)):
\(Rf'(3) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^+}\frac{[(3+h)^2+2]-11}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^+}\frac{6h+h^2}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^+}(6+h) = 6\).
Since \(Lf'(3) = Rf'(3) = 6\), the two one-sided derivatives agree.
f is differentiable at \(x=3\), with \(f'(3) = 6\).

Each piece is a polynomial, so f is differentiable at every \(x \ne 1\) whatever p and q are. Only \(x=1\) needs work, and there BOTH continuity and equality of the one-sided derivatives must hold.
Continuity at \(x=1\): \(\lim\limits_{x\to 1^-}(3-x) = 2\) and \(f(1) = p+q\), so
\(p + q = 2\) ... (i)
One-sided derivatives: \(Lf'(1) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^-}\frac{[3-(1+h)]-2}{h} = -1\), and for \(x\ge 1\), \(f'(x) = 2px+q\) gives \(Rf'(1) = 2p+q\). Equating,
\(2p + q = -1\) ... (ii)
Subtracting (i) from (ii): \(p = -3\), and then \(q = 2 - p = 5\).
Check: \(p+q = -3+5 = 2\) and \(2p+q = -6+5 = -1\). Both hold.
\(p = -3\), \(q = 5\).

Both pieces are polynomials, so only the join \(x=2\) matters, and there f must be continuous AND have equal one-sided derivatives.
Continuity at \(x=2\): \(\lim\limits_{x\to 2^-} px^3 = 8p\) and \(f(2) = 2^2 + q = 4+q\), so
\(8p = 4 + q\) ... (i)
One-sided derivatives: for \(x<2\), \(f'(x) = 3px^2\), so \(Lf'(2) = 12p\); for \(x\ge 2\), \(f'(x) = 2x\), so \(Rf'(2) = 4\). Equating,
\(12p = 4\), giving \(p = \frac{1}{3}\).
Substituting in (i): \(q = 8\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) - 4 = \frac{8}{3} - 4 = -\frac{4}{3}\).
\(p = \frac{1}{3}\), \(q = -\frac{4}{3}\).

Differentiability at \(x=1\) needs continuity there as well as equal one-sided derivatives.
Continuity at \(x=1\): \(f(1) = p(1)+q = p+q\) and \(\lim\limits_{x\to 1^+}\tan\left(\frac{\pi x}{4}\right) = \tan\frac{\pi}{4} = 1\), so
\(p + q = 1\) ... (i)
One-sided derivatives: for \(x\le 1\), \(f'(x) = p\), so \(Lf'(1) = p\). For \(1<x<2\), \(f'(x) = \frac{\pi}{4}\sec^{2}\left(\frac{\pi x}{4}\right)\), so \(Rf'(1) = \frac{\pi}{4}\sec^{2}\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{4}\times(\sqrt{2})^{2} = \frac{\pi}{4}\times 2 = \frac{\pi}{2}\).
Equating, \(p = \frac{\pi}{2}\), and from (i), \(q = 1 - \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{2-\pi}{2}\).
\(p = \frac{\pi}{2}\), \(q = \frac{2-\pi}{2}\).

Remove the moduli by splitting at their turning points \(x=-1\) and \(x=1\):
\(f(x) = -2x\) for \(x<-1\); \(f(x) = 2\) for \(-1\le x<1\); \(f(x) = 2x\) for \(x\ge 1\).
f is continuous everywhere (both \(|x+1|\) and \(|x-1|\) are), but continuity does not give differentiability, so test the corners.
At \(x=-1\) (here \(f(-1)=2\)): \(Lf'(-1) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^-}\frac{-2(-1+h)-2}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^-}\frac{-2h}{h} = -2\), while \(Rf'(-1) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^+}\frac{2-2}{h} = 0\). Since \(-2 \ne 0\), f is not differentiable at \(x=-1\).
At \(x=1\) (here \(f(1)=2\)): \(Lf'(1) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^-}\frac{2-2}{h} = 0\), while \(Rf'(1) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^+}\frac{2(1+h)-2}{h} = 2\). Since \(0 \ne 2\), f is not differentiable at \(x=1\).
On each of \((-\infty,-1)\), \((-1,1)\) and \((1,\infty)\) f is linear, hence differentiable there.
No. f is not differentiable for all \(x\in R\); it fails exactly at \(x=-1\) and \(x=1\).

Here \(f(2) = 2(2)-3 = 1\) and \(\lim\limits_{x\to 2^-}(x-1) = 1\), so f IS continuous at \(x=2\). Continuity is necessary but not sufficient, so compare the one-sided derivatives.
\(Lf'(2) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^-}\frac{f(2+h)-f(2)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^-}\frac{[(2+h)-1]-1}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^-}\frac{h}{h} = 1\).
\(Rf'(2) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^+}\frac{[2(2+h)-3]-1}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^+}\frac{2h}{h} = 2\).
Since \(Lf'(2) = 1 \ne 2 = Rf'(2)\), the one-sided derivatives are unequal.
f is not differentiable at \(x=2\) (though it is continuous there).

Here \(f(2) = 2^2+1 = 5\) and \(\lim\limits_{x\to 2^-}(2x+1) = 5\), so f is continuous at \(x=2\); this alone does not settle differentiability.
\(Lf'(2) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^-}\frac{[2(2+h)+1]-5}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^-}\frac{2h}{h} = 2\).
\(Rf'(2) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^+}\frac{[(2+h)^2+1]-5}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^+}\frac{4h+h^2}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^+}(4+h) = 4\).
Since \(Lf'(2) = 2 \ne 4 = Rf'(2)\), the one-sided derivatives differ.
f is not differentiable at \(x=2\) (though it is continuous there).

Here \(f(1) = 5(1)-3(1)^2 = 2\) and \(\lim\limits_{x\to 1^-}(3-x) = 2\), so f is continuous at \(x=1\). Now compare the one-sided derivatives.
\(Lf'(1) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^-}\frac{[3-(1+h)]-2}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^-}\frac{-h}{h} = -1\).
\(Rf'(1) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^+}\frac{[5(1+h)-3(1+h)^2]-2}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^+}\frac{-h-3h^2}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\to 0^+}(-1-3h) = -1\).
Since \(Lf'(1) = Rf'(1) = -1\), both one-sided derivatives agree.
f is differentiable at \(x=1\), with \(f'(1) = -1\).

The limit is a derivative in disguise. Since \(f(2)=4\), the numerator is \(4x - 2f(x)\). Add and subtract \(2f(2) = 8\) in it:
\(\lim\limits_{x\to 2}\frac{4x - 2f(x)}{x-2} = \lim\limits_{x\to 2}\frac{(4x-8) - 2[f(x)-f(2)]}{x-2}\)
\(= \lim\limits_{x\to 2}\frac{4(x-2)}{x-2} - 2\lim\limits_{x\to 2}\frac{f(x)-f(2)}{x-2}\)
\(= 4 - 2f'(2)\), because the second limit is precisely \(f'(2)\).
Putting \(f'(2) = 1\): \(4 - 2(1) = 2\).
The limit is \(2\).

\(y = \frac{e^{x}}{\sqrt{x}}\). By the quotient rule, with \(\frac{d}{dx}(\sqrt{x}) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\):
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sqrt{x}\cdot e^{x} - e^{x}\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}}{(\sqrt{x})^{2}} = \frac{e^{x}\left(2x-1\right)}{2x\sqrt{x}}\).
At \(x=1\): \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{e^{1}(2-1)}{2(1)\sqrt{1}} = \frac{e}{2}\).
\(\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=1} = \frac{e}{2}\).
